content: Joint pain, medically referred to as arthralgia (derived from the Greek words arthromeaning joint and -algos meaning pain), can arise from a variety of causes. These include trauma, infections, inflammatory processes, degeneration of bone or cartilage, adverse reactions to medications, or deposition of crystals within the joint. It is important to distinguish between arthralgia and arthritis, as the former refers to joint pain without inflammation, while the latter specifically involves inflammatory processes. As an orthopedic resident, your role is to thoroughly evaluate patients presenting with joint pain, localize the source of the discomfort, and identify the underlying pathophysiological cause. This requires a comprehensive differential diagnosis and a detailed review of the patient’s medical history. Joint pain can result from a broad range of conditions, including degenerative or destructive processes such as arthritis or sports-related injuries, inflammation of periarticular tissues like bursitis, or other systemic issues such as infections or reactions to vaccinations. Broadly, joint pain can be categorized into three main types: 1. Inflammatory arthritis: This type of joint pain is primarily caused by inflammation affecting structures such as the synovium, synovial cavity, or entheses. 2. Non-inflammatory arthritis: This type arises from structural or mechanical changes within the joint, rather than inflammation. 3. Arthralgia: This refers to joint tenderness or pain without any detectable joint abnormalities. Certain causes of joint pain can be life-threatening if not promptly addressed.
